video_title: Possible Bad News & Good Buying Opportunities Ahead
gist: Ed Yardeni (recorded Oct 26) flags four near-term risks (Middle East/Iran re-escalation and oil spike, sticky inflation forcing two more Fed hikes, midterm partisanship, AI-funding jitters) that could cause a pullback he would treat as a buying opportunity, while keeping a 7,900 S&P 500 year-end target (cut in September). He highlights analysts' forward earnings outrunning his own bold path ($500/share already in 2028 estimates vs. his 2030), falling P/Es (forward earnings +31% YTD vs. forward P/E -13.5%), and a 'G-shaped' boomer-driven consumer.

themes.theme: Four Halloween frights as buying opportunities

insights.claim: Ed Yardeni expects a possible stock market pullback driven by four risks: re-escalation of the Middle East war with Iran, oil-driven sticky inflation pushing the Fed to hike, post-midterm partisan conflict, and AI-trade funding jitters, and he would treat such a pullback as a buying opportunity.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Bias toward buying dips rather than de-risking.

insights.claim: Oil spiked to $120 a barrel early in the Middle East war, settled around $100, fell to the mid-$70s-$80s in summer and has climbed back to about $100, while the stock market has been fairly blasé about $100 oil.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Market tolerance of $100 oil limits damage unless a new spike occurs.

insights.claim: Yardeni says another oil spike cannot be ruled out because inventory stockpiles are down and the IRGC is unlikely to agree to a deal with the US, but he would buy that pullback since the blockaded Iranian economy is imploding and re-escalation would further degrade Iran's military.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Geopolitical oil shocks historically have been buying opportunities.

insights.claim: Yardeni notes the US president has talked about heating up the Iran conflict again after the midterms.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Post-November 3 is a window for renewed oil risk.

insights.claim: Yardeni expects two more Fed rate hikes in the next 6 to 12 months to take back the 75 basis points of cuts made last year, which he did not think were warranted, and says the market shares that view.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Tightening bias is priced; risk is if it proves insufficient.

insights.claim: Yardeni says it is not clear two rate hikes will be enough given the Fed's inflation problem, especially if oil prices stay higher for longer.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Upside rate risk is the tail for equities.

insights.claim: The 10-year Treasury yield reversed back to about 5% after an October scare, as buyers stepped in at a 5% handle amid an AI-jitters flight to safety, easing fears of 5.5%-6%; Yardeni expects 5% or less over the next 12 months.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: 5% looks like a ceiling where buyers emerge.

insights.claim: The 13-week change in the 10-year yield had become extended to the upside relative to the Citigroup Economic Surprise Index and has since moved back into line.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Useful gauge for when yield spikes are overdone.

insights.claim: Last week's rally in interest-rate-sensitive sectors (healthcare, real estate, utilities, financials) reflected the bond yield taking a breather back to 5%.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Rate-sensitive sectors trade inversely to 10-year yield moves.

themes.theme: AI funding jitters and credit discipline

insights.claim: Yardeni says last week's stock decline stemmed from concern over whether there is enough capital to fund AI companies' expansion ambitions, with Meta's announcement that it needs more capital hurting the Magnificent 7.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Capital availability, not demand, is the market's AI worry now.

insights.claim: Yardeni views rising investment-grade and high-yield CDS spreads on AI-related credits as healthy, arguing that a discriminating bond market is better than one that funds the AI story willy-nilly.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Wider AI credit spreads are discipline, not a systemic warning.

insights.claim: Yardeni expects the Anthropic IPO to go well and raise large sums that could help fund continued expansion and data centers.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: A successful IPO could ease AI-funding fears.

insights.claim: Yardeni cut his year-end S&P 500 target to 7,900 on September 15 due to these risks but still expects a Santa Claus rally and calls it a bull market, recommending investors stay fully invested.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Cautious tactically, bullish structurally.

insights.claim: Year to date as of Friday, the S&P 500 ex-Magnificent 7 is up 13.1%, the S&P 500 is up 11.4%, and the Magnificent 7 are up 6.2%, though breadth measured by percent of companies outperforming has narrowed.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: The 'impressive 493' have led this year.

insights.claim: S&P 500 forward earnings are up about 31% year to date while the index is up 11.4% and the forward P/E is down 13.5%, led by a significant drop in information technology's P/E.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Absent a recession, stocks are getting cheaper.

insights.claim: Analyst consensus already puts S&P 500 earnings at $500 per share for 2028, versus Yardeni's own projection of $500 per share by 2030, which at a 20x multiple implies 10,000 on the S&P 500.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Street is more bullish than the reputedly most bullish strategist; possible upside to his targets.

insights.claim: Yardeni notes 2026 S&P 500 earnings estimates were boosted by mark-to-market gains at Alphabet and Amazon, which he discounts, but the 2027 consensus has already reached his 2027 forecast and he may have to turn more bullish.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Earnings revisions are running unusually positive.
insights.quote: we might have to turn more bullish, believe it or not

insights.claim: Forward earnings for the S&P 500, S&P 400 and S&P 600 are all at record highs, indicating broad earnings strength across market caps.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Small and mid caps share in earnings growth.

insights.claim: Yardeni says analysts are good at anticipating earnings unless a recession hits, and he does not expect a recession over the forecast period.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Consensus earnings deserve weight absent recession signals.

themes.theme: Politics, global allocation and the G-shaped consumer

insights.claim: Yardeni notes betting markets and polls suggest Democrats will win the House and possibly the Senate in the November 3 midterms; divided government is typically market-friendly, but worse partisanship raises risks of longer, more painful debt-ceiling crises and shutdowns.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Gridlock good, but fiscal brinkmanship tail risk rises.

insights.claim: About a week ago Yardeni moved from overweighting global equities back to market weight (effectively overweight the US at 65% of MSCI market cap) and within non-US prefers EMXC over Europe, which looks dodgy.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Shift toward US and EM ex-China, away from Europe.

insights.claim: Yardeni says China's market is in significant free fall, with the real estate developer stock index breaking below support, which could be the next black swan.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Avoid China; watch property-sector contagion.

insights.claim: Yardeni describes a 'G-shaped' economy in which wealthy baby boomers, who own homes and financial assets, have low locked-in mortgages and benefit from higher money market rates, keep consumer spending resilient and support young adults, about 30% of whom live at home.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Consumer spending is insulated from the labor cycle and higher rates.

insights.claim: Yardeni argues boomer spending power contributes to the affordability crisis by helping keep prices higher.
insights.speaker: Ed Yardeni
insights.so_what: Wealth-effect demand adds to sticky inflation.
